title: Stoney Creek murder investigation reveals more details including a dispute over mould
subtitle: Brekka, with his bristling arsenal of weapons, wasn't known to police. He had no record. He must have had a trigger temper though, writes Rosie DiManno.
article: The police robot entered the house through the shattered front door. It "saw" two Carbine pistols, grasped one and took it to officers waiting outside at a distance, returned to extract the other, obediently delivered that one too. Both Scorpion pistols and a DPMS Panther Arms rifle, also recovered from the scene, are prohibited firearms in Canada. Scattered around were dozens of cartridge cases, magazines and damaged bullets.

The robot "searched" the area, opened a foyer door that led to the garage and relayed video showing a man lying on the ground in the garage. An officer, again from a distance, asked the man to make a movement, any movement, and medical assistance would be provided. The man didn't move even a tic.
The robot, moonlighting from its primary job as a remotely manipulated bomb disposal unit, trundled into the garage, grabbed the man by the left foot. No response.

There's lots of video, as it would turn out. But the key footage of events that preceded arrival by Hamilton Police at this residence on Jones Road in Stoney Creek on May 27, 2023, was retrieved from the home security camera installed by this dead man. That, along with security video from nearby homes and civilian cellphone video shot by neighbourhood residents, told on him - the 57-year-old man who owned the house.

The owner and a male tenant were in the garage arguing. The owner carried a rifle. The tenant raised his arms. Two shots were fired and the tenant fell to the ground. A second tenant, female, ran into the camera frame, rushed to the fallen man, then tried to flee. But the owner chased her down the driveway, continued to discharge his weapon. She collapsed backwards onto the road.

Carissa MacDonald, a 27-year-old educational assistant at St. Michael Catholic Elementary School and her 28-year-old fiancé, Aaron Stone, an apprentice electrician - they'd been planning their wedding and were scheduled to move out of their basement apartment within days - lay dead, slain in an explosion of gunfire that arose, investigators would learn, from a heated dispute over mould in the basement apartment.

"They were definitely not squatters," Det.-Sgt. Steve Bereziuk, from Hamilton's homicide squad and lead investigator, told the Star, referring to erroneous rumours at the time that the couple had been illegally occupying the premises, withholding rent. "They had always paid their rent on time and had given notice that they were leaving on June 1."

The owner, Terry Brekka - he lived upstairs - would barricade himself inside the house in a four-hour standoff with police that ended with Brekka killed, shot by an officer's Heckler and Koch rifle. That officer was on Monday formally cleared of any wrongdoing by the Special Investigations Unit. The report, released by SIU director Joseph Marino, is extraordinarily detailed.

Brekka, according to the report, had a drinking problem and a history of arguing, even threatening, his tenants over money. In this confrontation, he'd first shouted at MacDonald, demanding extra money. "Okay, you've got one second to pay," Brekka warned before left momentarily, then returned with the rifle. MacDonald screamed several times, said she'd give him the money, and told someone she'd been speaking to on the phone to call the cops. The phone was dropped, shots were heard. At least four people, witnesses to the shooting, called 911. But by the time police arrived in force, including an armoured tactical vehicle with ramrod extended, the couple were already deceased.

In the ensuing hours, police attempted to communicate with Brekka. At one point he asked, over the phone, if MacDonald and Stone were dead. Told they were, Brekka said he was sorry and asked police to convey his apology to the victims' families. In another communication, through a family member, he demanded police remove their armoured vehicle from his driveway. They didn't but did reverse it further away. It provided shelter from possible gunfire and also could block the shooter from attempting escape.

"Our tactical team used that vehicle for their own protection," says Bereziuk, "and to protect the public, prevent the shooter from going out on the street with his weapon. I believe that vehicle saved lives."

Brekka continued to have phone conversations with members of his family, repeatedly apologized for what he'd done and said he didn't expect to emerge from this situation alive. By that point police learned that Brekka was the registered owner of multiple handguns and rifles. They were understandably wary.

The cop who would afterwards be designated the subject officer by the SIU, was among those inside the armoured vehicle. At about 10:10 p.m. Brekka fired multiple rounds from inside the house in the direction of the vehicle. Two minutes later, another barrage from Brekka. The subject officer, positioned behind the turret hatch of the armoured vehicle, took aim at a hole in the front door through which it appeared the gunfire was coming and fired a single round from his HK416 rifle. The shooting from inside the house instantly stopped. Brekka was mortally wounded.
He did, however, make it to the garage through an interior door. Which is where his body would be found, lying facedown on the floor.
Three bodies, two completely innocent victims.
"This one's very disturbing," said Bereziuk, who's seen plenty of homicide wreckage. "Because there were no warning signs, so no ability for us to intervene.
"He just executed them."

Four months later, the homicide team is still trying to put together the pieces, their own investigation unable to rev up until their SIU had completed theirs and still very much open. The why of it, the murderous waste of it, Bereziuk is trying to figure out. "Maybe we'll never have the answer."
There were no reasonable grounds, as SIU director Marino concluded, to believe the subject officer committed any criminal offence. Lethal force was warranted, given that the cops were under fire.
There were no reasonable grounds, as anybody would conclude from the evidence, for Brekka to have gone spectacularly and monstrously violent in a heartbeat.

A double homicide. A couple with a whole life ahead of them, loved by family and friends, brutally gunned down over a conversation about mould that had apparently segued into discussion about the state of the rental unit. Brekka not happy with it, demanded extra money before they left.

"How does it escalate so quickly and to such lethal force?" Bereziuk asked aloud at the time. "It's a perfect storm of tragedy in this case because you can't predict something like this and you can't prevent it. Because nobody was on our radar, at least for the Hamilton police. It makes it difficult to understand how things can happen, certainly with respect to a landlord-tenant dispute."
Brekka, with his bristling arsenal of weapons, wasn't known to police. He had no record. He must have had a trigger temper, though. Who really knows what lies beneath?
"These are not people that this should happen to," Bereziuk had told a press conference after the horrific event. Of course it shouldn't happen to anybody but you'll take his meaning.

"They're not involved in any level of criminality or lifestyle that may lead to an incident like this. They are truly innocent victims, hardworking people, young people. They were engaged to be married. And this is a very tragic incident."
The couple had a dog, Max. The night of the murders, he escaped to a nearby home. But there was no escape for his human parents. They never stood a chance.
